newsitem.title: FRENCH POLYNESIA: French restore Mururoa atoll after N-tests.
newsitem.headline: French restore Mururoa atoll after N-tests.

text.p: Mururoa, the palm-fringed South Pacific atoll which became France's nuclear testing ground for three decades, is quietly being returned to its natural state of coconut palms and sand.
Since 1966, the idyllic atoll has witnessed 140 underground nuclear tests -- the final six rushed through last year in the face of widespread international opposition.
But now the military and scientific buildings are being torn down and salvageable equipment shipped off. A road and an airstrip is being left to be broken up and taken over by nature over time.

"We will depart after returning Mururoa to its natural state, leaving the atoll as we found it when we arrived 30 years ago," General Michel Boileau, the French military officer responsible for the clean-up job, told reporters allowed a rare glimpse of the remote and secret base.

Last year, as France wrapped up its much-criticised final series of tests on Mururoa and Fangataufa atolls, a French foreign ministry spokesman suggested, half in jest, that they could become a Club Mediterranee holiday resort.
Club Med responded it might look at the idea "if the area does not pose a risk to the lives of our staff and clients".
But France has since ruled out any development whatever on the isolated atoll around a turquoise lagoon, concluding that costs would be too high, Boileau said.
To avoid renewed global criticism over the controversial tests, officials have instead decided to restore the atolls as much as possible to their original state.
General Boileau said about 1,000 workers were involved in the demolition work, about a quarter of which was now completed. He said the task would be completed in mid-1998.
"Proposals for touristic, industrial or fishing projects ran into a simple reality: This atoll is isolated, far away from everything," he said.

"Simply to maintain the installations would cost some 100 million francs ($20 million) a year minimum....With such financial constraints, it is obvious that no economically viable project will ever see the light of day on Mururoa, so we are therefore going to abandon it."
He said France settled on dismantling the island's facilities for fear critics of its nuclear tests would seize on the atolls' condition to renew sniping at Paris.

Australia and New Zealand spearheaded global protests against the French testing series last year. France has foresworn all future testing and signed the Rarotonga Treaty making the South Pacific a nuclear-free zone.

Boileau said radiation levels would be permanently monitored on the atoll after the French military left and visitors would be allowed free access, although the army would reserve the right to keep an eye on things.
"It would be out of the question to let people do whatever they wanted -- for example, digging," he said.

The tests were staged in deep shafts drilled into basalt beneath the atolls' coral base. Though the blasts were said to melt surrounding rock, encapsulating any radioactive wastes, the military sounded like it did not want to take any chances.

Environmental groups have argued that surrounding waters could be contaminated by gradual leakage of radioactive material, but French officials insist there are only minimal radioactivity levels which pose no risk to health.
